name: Transconjunctival blepharoplasty / fat repositioning

lead: In this surgery the lower eyelid is opened from the inside, so there is no visible scar, and fat that forms under-eye bags is moved down over the orbital rim to fill the tear trough instead of being removed.
Published evidence comes mostly from surgeon case series and retrospective comparisons.

paras: Orbital fat pedicles are released and repositioned into a pocket over the cheek bone area to smooth the lid-cheek transition. The inner-lid approach is usually used when there is little excess skin.

As with eyelid surgery generally, swelling and bruising are common, and eyelid malposition is a reported risk; canthal support techniques may be used to reduce it. It is a surgical procedure performed by qualified surgeons.

lead: Transconjunctival blepharoplasty is lower-eyelid surgery performed through an incision on the inner surface of the eyelid, leaving no external scar. When combined with fat repositioning, orbital fat that causes lower-lid bags is moved over the orbital rim to fill the tear trough groove rather than being removed.[1][2][3]

Wikipedia notes the transconjunctival approach is usually used when there is little excess skin, and that additional procedures may be needed if skin laxity is present.[1] Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series and retrospective comparisons rather than randomized trials.

paras: Wikipedia describes transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty as an inner-lid incision approach that avoids an external scar, in contrast with a transcutaneous incision below the lashes, which allows skin removal.[1] The procedure is typically outpatient and takes one to three hours, with swelling and bruising resolving over several weeks.[1]

A 1995 article described that conventional lower blepharoplasty that removes lower-lid fat can create a hollowed contour deformity, and described arcus marginalis release with fat preservation as an alternative.[4] A 2000 paper described transposing orbital fat pedicles into a subperiosteal pocket over the orbital rim to treat the tear trough.[5]

A 2013 retrospective single-surgeon comparison looked at transposing fat to the subperiosteal versus supraperiosteal plane.[2] Other reports describe intra-SOOF dissection approaches with initial outcomes, and fat repositioning combined with grafting for sunken upper eyelids in Asian patients.[6][7] A review discusses types of tear trough anatomy and treatment options,[3] and an MRI study examined orbital changes with age contributing to lower-lid prominence.[8]
Surgeons' survey data on technique trends exist for members of the American Society of Ophthalmic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.[9]

Evidence is limited to retrospective reviews and case series such as those above;[2][6][7] the sources reviewed identified no randomized controlled trials of lower-lid fat repositioning. A registered trial concerns medial fat pad preservation in upper eyelid blepharoplasty.[10]
Wikipedia notes canthopexy or canthoplasty may be used to reduce eyelid malposition risk.[1] Swelling and bruising are common after surgery.[1]

timeline.event: Karl Ferdinand von Graefe coins the term blepharoplasty.[1]
Arcus marginalis release with orbital fat preservation described.[4]
Transconjunctival orbital fat repositioning into a subperiosteal pocket described.[5]
